claims.text: Protective oxide formation and persistence in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C is controlled by preferential oxidation of Al.
An Al-containing alloy above a critical Al concentration forms a slow-growing alumina scale.
The alumina scale is adherent and inhibits further oxygen ingress.
CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si or Mn form less-stable oxides that tend to crack or spall.
An interfacial Al2O3 layer coherent with the underlying alloy microstructure mediates protective behavior.
Oxide scales on the Mn- or Si-containing variants have inferior adhesion and coherence.
Thermodynamic and kinetic driving forces preferentially oxidize Al.
Preferential Al oxidation produces a stable, low-growth, adherent alumina scale.
The alumina scale acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
Mn- or Si-containing variants form mixed or otherwise less-protective oxides.
Oxides on Mn- or Si-containing variants grow faster than the proposed alumina scale.
Thermal-expansion and bonding mismatches make the Mn- or Si-associated oxide scales prone to cracking or spallation.
Alloys with sufficient Al will consistently develop a thin, continuous, coherent alumina-based layer during the specified exposure.
The alumina-based layer will persist during high-temperature oxidative exposure.
Under the same conditions, Mn- or Si-containing variants will develop thicker, less-adherent scales that crack or spall.
The proposed behavior applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
The prediction may not apply at substantially lower temperatures or to substantially different processing microstructures.

Failure of high-Al variants to show a statistically significant improvement in scale thickness, coherence, adhesion, or spallation relative to Mn or Si variants would falsify preferential Al oxidation as the governing explanation.
